newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore dollar slides to 30-month low.
newsitem.headline: Singapore dollar slides to 30-month low.

text.p: The Singapore dollar slid to a 30-month low of 1.4593 in mid-afternoon trade on Thursday, foreign exchange dealers said.
The last time the Singapore dollar was at this level was in December 1994. At 0800 GMT, it had recovered slightly and was being quoted at 1.4565/75.
Dealers said the U.S. funds were buying dollars against the Sing in the afternoon.

"We heard U.S. houses have been the main buyers. Some U.S. funds had sold the dollar at around 1.4450/60 yesterday as they thought the level may be capped but now it seems they are buying back," said a dealer with a European bank.
Dealers said the Sing started weakening against the dollar in early morning trade. Stop losses were triggered after the Sing broke support at the pyschological 1.4500 level.
"The market is a bit short on dollars. I would be buying dollars on dips as the dollar/Sing should head higher to 1.47 in the near term," said the European bank dealer.

Dealers said the local currency was just playing a catch up game as the rest of the regional currencies like the Malaysian ringgit and the Indonesia rupiah have weakened much more sharply against the greenback in the past week.
They also said the noticeable absence in the market of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the de facto central bank, would also encourage further slides in the Sing.
"There is no sign of the authorities checking rates. The Sing hasn't been at these levels for a long time, so the top is the limit," said a regional currencies trader.
He said local companies were mostly under-hedged in dollars. "There is some worry about corporates that they may be short of dollars by year-end when they need to repatriate profits."
Dealers said the MAS was likely to allow a weaker Sing dollar so it remained competitive against regional currencies.
They said current sentiment could send the Sing to a low of 1.5000, especially if regional currencies weaken further.

Song Seng Wun, regional economist with ABN AMBRO Hoare Govett Securities, said the Sing dollar exchange rate was determined by a trade-weighted basket of currencies of which regional currencies form about a third.
"If the regional currencies fall further, the MAS would have to tolerate a weaker Sing dollar to prevent it from appreciating more than its one or two percent a year against the greenback," he said.
However, regional currencies should regain some strength when exports in the region pick up, said Song, who expected the Sing to recover to around 1.4100 by year-end.
